===== WORLD 1 · LESSON what_poker_is · Your cards and the board =====

SUMMARY: Find the two cards that belong to you.
CAPTION: A new hand.
TEACH: Find your cards. Your private cards are the two beside your seat. The board is the group of cards everyone still playing can use. Look at where each group sits before reading the ranks.

===== WORLD 1 · LESSON chips_in_the_middle · Blinds and the pot =====

TASK w1_chips_starting_pot [drill] Read the two forced posts
CAPTION: The two marked seats have put in their starting amounts. Every other stack is still untouched. Read their two contributions before you read the total.
TEACH: The first two contributions Blinds are forced contributions: the small blind puts in 0.5 BB and the big blind puts in 1 BB before anyone chooses.
TEACH: Read the middle The pot is the chips in the middle, so add what both players have put in and leave out the chips still in their stacks.
Q: What is the total in the middle before anyone chooses what to do?
HINT [theoryOnly]: (none)
TABLE: Preflop | You 5s 8c | Pot 1.5 BB | To call 1 BB | Seat UTG | Active utg | Decision utg | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG 5s 8c stack 100 BB | HJ stack 100 BB | CO stack 100 BB | BTN dealer stack 100 BB | SB stack 99.5 BB post 0.5 BB | BB stack 99 BB post 1 BB
TRAIL: SB blind 0.5 BB · BB blind 1 BB
  - [wrong] 1 BB — Read the table again. The big blind put in 1 BB. Counting that seat alone leaves out the half chip unit at the other marked seat.
    BETTER ANSWER: 1.5 BB
  + [correct] 1.5 BB — Correct. The two forced amounts are 0.5 and 1 BB. Adding them gives the 1.5 BB already in the middle.
  - [wrong] 0.5 BB — Read the table again. The small blind put in 0.5 BB. The 1 BB from the other marked seat belongs in the same total.
    BETTER ANSWER: 1.5 BB

TASK w1_chips_matched_pot [drill] Count each contribution once

===== WORLD 1 · LESSON first_table_guide · First Table Guide =====

TASK first_table_guide_first_decision [drill] Decide with your coach
CAPTION: The player before you raised to 2.5 BB.
TEACH: Three choices. Fold gives up. Call matches the bet. Raise increases it. Raise to an amount means your total for that betting round reaches that amount. A reraise means raising an earlier raise; the first reraise is called a 3-bet. Two aces are the strongest starting hand. With the strongest hand you want more chips in the pot, so you raise.
Q: How will you play your aces?
HINT [theoryOnly]: (none)
TABLE: Preflop | You As Ac | Pot 4 BB | To call 2.5 BB | Seat CO | Active co | Decision co | Facts pocket pair
EFFECTIVE: HJ 100 · BTN 100 · SB 100 · BB 100
REASONING: principle value_vs_worse · alt call · edge moreValueFromWorse · stack_matters false · assumption none
SEATS: UTG folded stack 100 BB | HJ stack 97.5 BB raise 2.5 BB | CO As Ac stack 100 BB | BTN dealer stack 100 BB | SB stack 99.5 BB post 0.5 BB | BB stack 99 BB post 1 BB
TRAIL: SB blind 0.5 BB · BB blind 1 BB · An earlier player folds · The player before you raises to 2.5 BB
  - [wrong] Fold — Your aces can play. Folding aces to one raise gives up the strongest starting hand and the chance to win this pot.
    BETTER ANSWER: Raise to 7.5 BB
  - [suboptimal] Call [2.5 BB] — Calling keeps you in. Calling 2.5 BB keeps you in. Raising can get the player before you to pay more while you have the strongest hand.
    BETTER ANSWER: Raise to 7.5 BB
  + [correct] Raise to 7.5 BB — Raise with aces. With AA, a raise can get the earlier raiser to pay more with weaker pairs or strong aces. A call keeps the pot smaller against those hands.

===== WORLD 1 · LESSON cards_ranks_suits · Cards, ranks & suits =====

TASK cards_ranks_suits_theory [theory] The deck
CAPTION: A deck has 52 cards.
TEACH: Deck first. Hold'em uses a 52-card deck: 13 ranks across 4 suits. Numbers run from 2 up to 10. J means Jack, Q means Queen, K means King, and A means Ace.
TEACH LABELS: 52 cards, 13 ranks, 4 suits, 2 ... 10, J Q K A
TEACH TABLE: Preflop | You As Kd | Pot 1.5 BB | Seat BTN | Seat focus btn | Card focus hero_0, hero_1 | Center Ranks and suits | Facts no applicable hand facts
Q: What are the two parts of a card?
HINT [theoryOnly]: Each card combines one rank with one suit.
TABLE: Preflop | You As Kd | Pot 1.5 BB | Seat BTN | Seat focus btn | Center Ranks and suits | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG | HJ | CO | BTN dealer | SB post 0.5 BB | BB post 1 BB
  - [wrong] The rank value — Rank is one part. Rank names the value, but a card also has a suit.
    BETTER ANSWER: Rank and suit
  + [correct] Rank and suit — Both parts found. Rank names the value and suit names the symbol family.
  - [wrong] The suit symbol — Suit is one part. Suit names the symbol family, but a card also has a rank.
    BETTER ANSWER: Rank and suit

Ace is highest for now, so ace beats king in this drill.

===== WORLD 1 · LESSON what_poker_is_content · Stacks, all-in and the pot =====

TASK what_poker_is_pot_stack [theory] Pot and stack
SUMMARY: Separate chips in the middle from chips that still belong to a player.
TEACH: BB also counts chips. BB also measures chips. In a $1/$2 game, $200 is 100 BB.
TEACH: Pot and stack The pot is in the middle. Your stack stays at your seat.
Q: Which label shows the chips in the middle?
HINT [theoryOnly]: Compare the chips in the middle with the chips in front of you.
TABLE: Preflop | Pot 1.5 BB | Seat HJ | Seat focus hj, sb, bb | Tap utg, btn, bb | Center Pot vs stack | Empty board No board cards yet | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG | HJ stack 100 BB | CO | BTN dealer | SB post 0.5 BB | BB post 1 BB
TRAIL: SB blind 0.5 BB · BB blind 1 BB
  + [correct] Pot — Clean execution. The pot is the chips in the middle.
  - [wrong] Stack — Not quite. Your stack stays with your seat. The pot is the shared chips in the middle that everyone is playing for.
    BETTER ANSWER: Pot
  - [wrong] Blind — Read the deciding detail. The blind is one forced post. Once the 0.5 BB and 1 BB are in the middle, the pot names their combined total.
    BETTER ANSWER: Pot

TASK what_poker_is_all_in_meaning [drill] All-in meaning

CAPTION: You are all-in for 20 BB. CO called 20 BB and still has chips behind.
TEACH: All-in means no chips behind. 0 BB behind = all-in. Cards or folds still decide.
TEACH LABELS: 0 BB behind, 20 BB in, Cards still decide

HINT [theoryOnly]: All-in means one player has put in all remaining chips. The cards or folds still decide the pot.

    BETTER ANSWER: You put in all remaining chips
  + [correct] You put in all remaining chips — Correct table read. All-in means you committed all remaining chips. It does not automatically win the pot, because cards or folds still decide what happens next.
  - [wrong] Only the bigger stack matters now — Stack size still has a role, but not that role. CO has chips left. You put in your last chips. The hand still has to be decided.
    BETTER ANSWER: You put in all remaining chips

TASK what_poker_is_matched_chips_transfer [drill] Matched chips
SUMMARY: A short stack can only win the chips that were actually matched in front of it.
CAPTION: You put in your last 20 BB. CO calls 20 BB and still has chips left.
TEACH: Short stacks cannot win unmatched chips. Only matched chips count. CO's 80 BB behind stays out.
TEACH LABELS: Matched chips, 80 BB behind, Not contested
Q: How many chips can you win from CO in this hand?
HINT [theoryOnly]: Count how much each player put in for this hand.
TABLE: Preflop | Pot 41.5 BB | Seat HJ | Seat focus hj, co | Center Matched chips set the contest | Empty board No board cards yet | Facts no applicable hand facts

TRAIL: Blinds: 1.5 BB · UTG folds · You go all-in for 20 BB · CO calls, 20 BB total · BTN folds · SB folds · BB folds
  - [wrong] 100 BB — Too many chips counted. Your all-in caps CO’s contribution to the pot you can win at 20 BB. Any further chips CO bets against another player stay in a separate pot.
    BETTER ANSWER: 20 BB
  - [wrong] 0 BB — Matched already matters. You can win the 20 BB that CO matched. CO keeps the chips they did not put in.
    BETTER ANSWER: 20 BB
  + [correct] 20 BB — Correct matched-chips read. You can win the 20 BB CO matched. That limit stays fixed for this hand, even if CO bets more against another player.

TASK what_poker_is_side_pot_eligibility [drill] Which chips can you win?

===== WORLD 2 · LESSON hand_discipline_buckets · Hand buckets =====

TASK hand_discipline_buckets_intro [theory] Four buckets
CAPTION: Preflop starts by sorting the hand into a simple bucket.
TEACH: You are first in. Enter first voluntarily. Open means the first raise.
TEACH: Groups and seats, before a raise. T means ten. Suited means same suit (s); offsuit means different suits (o).

Sharky 6-max starting chart. Open means the first raise preflop.

Premium: AA–QQ, AK suited (UTG–BTN).

Strong: JJ–TT, AK offsuit, AQ suited, AJ suited (UTG–BTN).

Medium: AQ offsuit, AJ offsuit, KQ, AT (HJ–BTN).

Medium: 99–22, KJ, QJ, KT, QT (CO–BTN).

Weak: other hands (Fold).
TEACH: On BTN after a raise. BTN vs one HJ/CO open: call AQo, AJo, KQs, KQo, ATs, ATo, KJs, QJs. Fold other Medium and Weak hands.
Q: What should you name before the action?
HINT [theoryOnly]: Hand code writes the two ranks together. T means ten, s means suited, and o means offsuit.
TABLE: Preflop | You Ks Ts | Pot 1.5 BB | To call 1 BB | Seat CO | Active co | Decision co | Center Your turn | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG folded stack 100 BB | HJ folded stack 100 BB | CO Ks Ts stack 100 BB | BTN dealer stack 100 BB | SB stack 99.5 BB post 0.5 BB | BB stack 99 BB post 1 BB
TRAIL: SB blind 0.5 BB · BB blind 1 BB · UTG folds · HJ folds
REVIEW: Raising sets a higher price. Calling pays the price already set.

===== WORLD 2 · LESSON w2_narrow_three_bet · The narrow 3-bet =====

TASK w2_narrow_three_bet_intro [theory] One open ahead
CAPTION: Face one opening raise with nobody else in the pot.
TEACH: A 3-bet is a raise over the first raise. A 4-bet is a raise over a 3-bet; at micro stakes it usually means QQ+ or AK. Here HJ or CO opens once, and you act after them. Reraise AA, KK, QQ, and AK (suited or offsuit). Call with the other Strong hands: JJ, TT, AQs, and AJs. With Medium hands, call from BTN with AQo, AJo, KQs, KQo, ATs, ATo, KJs, or QJs. Fold the rest of Medium, including all Medium hands from CO, and fold Weak hands. This rule requires position and no other callers.
Q: What changes when you raise over an open?
HINT [theoryOnly]: (none)
TABLE: Preflop | You Ah Ac | Pot 4 BB | To call 2.5 BB | Seat CO | Active co | Decision co | Facts pocket pair
SEATS: UTG folded stack 100 BB | HJ stack 97.5 BB raise 2.5 BB | CO Ah Ac stack 100 BB | BTN dealer stack 100 BB | SB stack 99.5 BB post 0.5 BB | BB stack 99 BB post 1 BB
TRAIL: SB blind 0.5 BB · BB blind 1 BB · UTG folds · HJ raises to 2.5 BB
REVIEW: Raising sets a higher price. Calling pays the price already set.

===== WORLD 3 · LESSON w3_play_from_blinds · Play from the blinds =====

TASK w3_play_from_blinds_intro [theory] Two blinds, different choices
TEACH: Facing BTN. SB reraises Premium, Strong and HJ Medium. Fold CO Medium and Weak. "Defend your blind" means calling or reraising from SB or BB. From BB subtract your 1 BB post. Equity means pot share from wins and ties. A 1.5 BB call for 5.5 BB needs about 27%.
TEACH: Only the blinds remain. Blind versus blind means everyone folded to SB. SB acts before BB after the flop. An SB limp means completing the blind, usually worse than raising or folding. A raise to 3 BB makes BB pay 2 BB more. BB’s call ends preflop here.

===== WORLD 4 · LESSON call_price · Call price =====

TASK w4_price_intro [theory] Facing a price
CAPTION: When someone bets, they set your price to continue.
TEACH: Call 2 BB into a pot of 8 BB. Five calls cost 10 BB. One win returns 10 BB, so you break even at one in five. Middle pair means your private card matches the second-highest rank on the flop. Bottom pair means matching the lowest.
TEACH LABELS: 8 BB in the pot, 2 BB to call, 1 in 5
TEACH: Write the same chance as a percentage. One win in five is 20%. To call X into a pot of Y after the bet, you need to win at least X ÷ (X + Y) of the time when there are no ties or further bets.
TEACH LABELS: 1 in 5, 20%

===== WORLD 5 · LESSON board_texture_basics · Dry or wet board =====

TASK board_texture_basics_w5_texture_intro [theory] Board texture
CAPTION: Board texture asks how much the next cards can change.
TEACH: What can change? A dry board has few ways for the next card to change who leads. A wet board has many. When ranks sit close together or suits match, more hands can improve.
TEACH LABELS: Rank gaps, Suits
TEACH: Three of one suit. These three spades are called a monotone flop. A player with two more spades already has a flush.

===== WORLD 5 · LESSON w5_semi_bluff · Bet with a draw =====

TASK w5_semi_bluff_intro [theory] Two ways to win
CAPTION: You have a draw on the turn.
TEACH: Two ways to win. A semi-bluff is a bet with a draw. It can win when a better hand folds, or later when your draw hits. After BB checks to you here, checking behind gives you a free river. Compare what each choice wins and loses on average. Checking can earn the pot if the draw hits. When you bet, a fold wins the chips already in the middle. A call gives you a chance to win a bigger pot and costs you the bet when you miss. Count each good river once, even if it completes two draws.
Q: When can a bet earn more than a check?
HINT [theoryOnly]: Count the cards that complete the draw. Then compare the chance with the price.

HINT [theoryOnly]: Value bets to get called. Bluff candidates can bet to fold out better hands.

===== WORLD 6 · LESSON range_combo_counts · Count the combos =====

TASK w6_combo_counts_intro [theory] Why combo counts matter
CAPTION: Ranges are not just hand names. They also have combo counts.
TEACH: Families have counts. A combo is one exact two-card hand. Four aces times four kings gives 16 A-K combos. Four share a suit and 12 do not. A pocket pair has six ways to choose two of its four cards. A blocker is a known card, such as one you hold, that rules out any opponent combo containing it.
TEACH LABELS: 16 combos, 6 combos, Range density
Q: Why do combo counts matter?
HINT [theoryOnly]: First count the possible hands. To weigh a range, ask how often each one takes the action.
TABLE: Preflop | You Jc 9d | Pot 1.5 BB | To call 1 BB | Seat UTG | Active utg | Decision utg | Center Count combinations | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG Jc 9d stack 100 BB | HJ stack 100 BB | CO stack 100 BB | BTN dealer stack 100 BB | SB stack 99.5 BB post 0.5 BB | BB stack 99 BB post 1 BB
TRAIL: SB blind 0.5 BB · BB blind 1 BB
REVIEW: A hand family represents several different two-card combinations. Count them to see how much weight each family has.

===== WORLD 6 · LESSON w6_continuation_bet · After your preflop raise =====

TASK w6_continuation_bet_intro [theory] The next bet after a raise
CAPTION: CO raised and BB called, then checked the flop. Read the three ranks and suits first. Ask which weaker hands could pay a small bet and which draws BB could continue with.
TEACH: Continuation bet, or c-bet A flop continuation bet is a bet by the last preflop raiser. Against one caller who checks on a dry flop, a one-third-pot bet can get paid by worse hands. Connected two-tone flops give callers more ways to continue. On those flops, often check behind when you miss and have neither a good draw nor a reason to expect folds. Compare weaker calls with better folds before you bet.

===== WORLD 8 · LESSON short_stack_spots · Short-stack spots =====

TASK short_stack_spots_intro [theory] Effective stack at two depths
CAPTION: Compare a stack of 100 BB with a stack of 25 BB.
TEACH: Only chips both players can match count. With two players, 100 BB against 25 BB plays like 25 BB. A short stack means few big blinds left. Implied odds mean extra chips you might win later. Reverse implied odds mean extra chips you might lose if you improve and still trail. In a three-player pot, the main pot includes the chips everyone can match. A side pot is a separate pot for extra matched chips. Only live contributors can win it.
Q: How much can these two players put at risk against each other?
HINT [theoryOnly]: Low SPR means less money is left relative to the pot. Check your hand and the price before going all-in.
TABLE: Preflop | You Kh Qh | Pot 4 BB | To call 2.5 BB | Seat BTN | Active btn | Decision btn | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG folded stack 100 BB | HJ folded stack 100 BB | CO stack 22.5 BB raise 2.5 BB | BTN dealer Kh Qh stack 100 BB | SB stack 99.5 BB post 0.5 BB | BB stack 99 BB post 1 BB
TRAIL: SB blind 0.5 BB · BB blind 1 BB · UTG folds · HJ folds · CO raises to 2.5 BB
REVIEW: You can risk only 25 BB against a player with 25 BB.

===== WORLD 8 · LESSON format_pressure · 6-max vs full ring =====

===== WORLD 9 · LESSON survival_pressure_basics · Chips and prizes =====

TASK w9_survival_intro [theory] Chips and prizes
CAPTION: Chips and expected prize money are different measures.
TEACH: Chips and prizes EV stands for expected value. It is your average result if you make the same choice many times. Chip EV counts chips. Prize EV counts prize money. Your run ends if you lose your stack. Near a payout, a small gain in chips can cost prize value. M = stack / (SB + BB + antes for one lap). Green is 20 or more. Yellow is 10 to under 20. Red is below 10.
Q: What does EV describe?
HINT [theoryOnly]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
REVIEW: EV includes winning and losing outcomes, weighted by their chances; one lost hand can come from a profitable decision.

TEACH: A close river call When a call can bust you, check both costs. First work out the chip price from the pot and call. Then compare your win rate with the prize model.

===== WORLD 9 · LESSON bubble_risk_premium · Bubble risk premium =====

TASK w9_bubble_intro [theory] What does a call cost?
CAPTION: The money bubble is the last stage before those left win a prize.
TEACH: What does a call cost? Equity is your share of a pot on average. A tie gets its share too. Near a prize, a call that could bust you may need more equity than the chip price asks for. The gap is the risk premium. In this example the payout model requires 55% equity and the chip price requires 40%. A stack that can bust yours covers you. Check the rest of the stacks and the prizes too.
Q: What is this example's risk premium?
HINT [theoryOnly]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
REVIEW: Subtract the chip threshold from the payout threshold: 55%-40%=15 percentage points.

TASK w9_bubble_premium_gap [drill] The extra cost of a call
CAPTION: You need to win 36% of the time for chips. The prize model needs 51%.
Q: How much extra equity does the call need?
HINT [theoryOnly]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  - [wrong] 36 points — Look again. 36% is the chip price. Using it as the gap overstates the extra cost.
    BETTER ANSWER: 15 points
  + [correct] 15 points — Correct. The gap from 36% to 51% is 15 points.
  - [wrong] 51 points — Look again. 51% is the whole target. Treating it as a gap counts the chip price twice.
    BETTER ANSWER: 15 points

===== WORLD 10 · LESSON player_type_basics · Who is at the table =====

TASK w10_player_type_intro [theory] How players act
CAPTION: Watch how often players call, bet or fold.
TEACH: How players act A nit folds often. A loose-passive player calls and rarely raises. A calling station calls too often. An aggressive player bets and raises often. LAG means loose-aggressive, a player who enters many hands and raises often. A maniac is an extreme case who frequently raises even weak hands. A steal means raising first to win the blinds. An underbluffer seldom bluffs. A 3-bet is a raise over an open. A c-bet is a flop bet from the preflop raiser.
Q: Which clue is most useful over time?
HINT [theoryOnly]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
REVIEW: Several hands can show how often a player folds, calls or bets. You can use that read in the next hand.

===== WORLD 11 · LESSON table_trigger_reads · In-session trigger reads =====

TASK w11_trigger_intro [theory] Trigger-first routine
CAPTION: Read the table, then pick one response.
TEACH: Trigger-first routine A multiway pot has at least three live players. A c-bet is a flop bet by the preflop raiser. A 3-bet is a raise over an open. Against one opponent, flop SPR is the smaller stack divided by the flop pot. An overpair is a pocket pair above every board rank.
Q: Flop pot 6, stack left 12: what SPR?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Seat CO | Center Hypothetical example | Empty board Use the stated premise | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG | HJ | CO | BTN dealer | SB | BB
  + [correct] 2 — Correct. SPR is 12/6=2. You have twice the pot left to play.
  - [wrong] 6 — Look again. 6 BB is the pot size, not the ratio. The 12 BB stack is twice that pot.
    BETTER ANSWER: 2
  - [wrong] 12 — Look again. 12 BB is the stack left, not the ratio. Divide it by the 6 BB pot.
    BETTER ANSWER: 2

===== WORLD 12 · LESSON decision_over_outcome · Decision quality over outcome =====

TASK w12_decision_quality_intro [theory] Process first
CAPTION: A good choice can lose. A poor choice can win.
TEACH: Process first EV means expected value: the average gain or loss over many repeats. An out is a card that makes a losing hand win. On the turn, count clean outs, not cards that help the other player more. A river call needs a win rate high enough for its price. A c-bet is a flop bet from the preflop raiser. Variance means short-term results naturally swing, and downswings are stretches of losses that can happen even when your decisions are sound.
Q: What should you test after a lucky win?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Seat CO | Center Hypothetical example | Empty board Use the stated premise | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG | HJ | CO | BTN dealer | SB | BB
  + [correct] The price and range you faced — Correct. A lucky river can hide a bad call. The old price and the likely hands decide if it had value.
  - [wrong] The size of the pot you won — Look again. A large pot can come from a weak call. Pot size alone does not show if the price was good.
    BETTER ANSWER: The price and range you faced
  - [wrong] How happy the win made you — Look again. A good feeling is real, but it does not show if your hand had enough wins for the bet.
    BETTER ANSWER: The price and range you faced

TASK w12_good_fold_bad_result [drill] A new river decision
CAPTION: Last orbit, BB showed a bluff after you folded. On this river BB bets 12 into 16. In 20 similar spots, BB had 3 missed KQ/QT and 17 Ax or sets. JJ beats the misses; it loses to the value hands.
TEACH: A new river decision One shown card can help you learn. It does not replace a larger group of showdowns. On the river, there is no next card to save a weak call.

===== WORLD 12 · LESSON tilt_reset_protocol · Tilt reset protocol =====

TASK w12_tilt_reset_intro [theory] Reset in under 20s
CAPTION: What happened in the last hand can affect your next choice.
TEACH: Reset in under 20s Tilt is when anger, fear or stress starts to steer your play. A quick reset can protect the next hand. You can note the feeling, slow your next choice and check the table facts. If focus does not return, you can leave the session. A pause does not change pot odds.

  - [wrong] The odds on the next board — Look again. The next cards do not change due to your mood. Only the care you take with the choice can change.

TASK w12_confidence_intro [theory] Calm assertive posture
CAPTION: A river example starts with 16 BB in the middle. A rival adds 8 BB, making the pot 24 BB.
TEACH: Calm assertive posture Confidence does not mean a larger bet. Start by reading the chips already in the pot. Your own chips enter only if you call. An overpair is a pocket pair above the top board card. A bluff-catcher beats bluffs but loses to value hands. Call price equals the call divided by the pot after your call.
Q: What is the call price?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Seat CO | Center Hypothetical example | Empty board Use the stated premise | Facts no applicable hand facts
SEATS: UTG | HJ | CO | BTN dealer | SB | BB

  - [wrong] 33.3% — Look again. A call would make the 24 BB pot grow to 32 BB. Dividing by 24 leaves out your own call.
    BETTER ANSWER: 25%
  - [wrong] 50% — Look again. Calling 8 BB can win more than 8. The final pot is 32 BB, so 50% is far too high.
    BETTER ANSWER: 25%
